title: When a website project is also a product project

faqs.question: Why should a site and a product share words?
faqs.answer: The buyer learns the names of the objects on the homepage, then looks for those names after login. If the site says workspace and the product says project, they hesitate at the door. Pick one noun, write the definition, and change both surfaces in the same week when the name changes.

faqs.question: How do you catch a seam?

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Website and product design together means one brand, not two projects that share a wordmark. If the thing you sell is software, the site and the product should share type, color, and the words for the same objects. A buyer who moves from the homepage to the app should feel they stayed in the same place. A seam at the login is a second company you did not mean to introduce.

Start by naming the objects once. Then use those names on the marketing page and in the interface. The visuals follow the words. If the words diverge, no palette will hide it.

## One vocabulary

List the nouns the product actually uses. A lead, a board, a shipment, a position, a team. Write the definition in a sentence a stranger could almost use. The website may only show three of them. It must not invent friendlier synonyms that the product then contradicts.

If the site says “workspace” and the product says “project,” the buyer will hesitate at the door, looking for the workspace they were promised. Pick one. Change the site or change the product, and do it on purpose. A glossary hidden in a help doc does not fix a homepage button.

Got Next and Leadly, public Hanabi product interfaces, are built around a job and a small set of actions. The marketing page for a product like that should describe those actions in the same verbs the buttons use. “Create the next item” on the site, and a button that says “Create,” is a coherent path. A site that says “unlock your potential” and a button that says “New record” is a handoff between strangers.

Trade Moai, a public trading interface concept, is a different density. A marketing page for a tool like that can be quieter than the product, because the product has to hold a working screen. Quiet is not a different language. The names of the objects on the dense screen should appear, accurately, in the explanation. Do not simplify a real object into a metaphor you will abandon at login.

Write the list where both teams can see it. Designers in Figma, engineers in the repo, and whoever edits the site. When a name changes, it changes in both places in the same week. A rename that ships in the product and waits a month on the site is a seam you chose.

## Type, color, and the feeling of one house

Use the same type for the marketing headlines and the product’s primary text, or a deliberate, documented pair. Two unrelated faces say two vendors. The sprint’s small palette should style the action button in the product and the action button on the site. If the product needs a denser UI color for charts, add it as a product color with a job, not as a surprise theme.

People decide they are in the right place quickly. Nielsen Norman Group’s 2011 article on [how long users stay on web pages](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) reports that users often leave within 10 to 20 seconds unless the value is clear early. The product’s first screen after login is under the same pressure. It should confirm the promise the site just made, in the same voice. A dashboard that looks like a different brand forces them to re-learn trust at the worst moment.

Space can differ. A marketing page can be more open. A product screen can be tighter because the job is repeated. The difference should be density, not personality. If you removed the logo, a regular user should still feel the family resemblance in type, color, and wording.

Motion, if you use it, should follow one rule. Hanabi uses Motion where it helps, and keeps a reduced-motion path. A marketing site full of scroll effects and a product that is abrupt, or the reverse, feels accidental. Pick the rule in the shared note. “Menus move. Data does not bounce.” Then keep it.

## What the site may simplify, and what it must not

The site may show fewer features. It may use a calmer crop of the interface. It may explain one workflow instead of the whole map. Simplifying the count is good. Simplifying the truth is not. Do not show a concept screen you have no plan to ship. Do not name a control that does not exist. The screenshot on the homepage should be a real state, or a faithful composition of real states, labeled honestly if it is composed.

Do not promise a pace the product does not have. If the site says “instant” and the product has a queue, the seam will be felt in the first minute of use, which is a support ticket and a trust problem. Describe the real interval.

The site may have pages the product will never have: the story of the company, the pricing, the security note, the intro call. Those pages should still use the vocabulary and the type. Pricing in a different visual system looks like a partner’s landing page. It is a common accident when “the marketing site” and “the app” are procured separately. Buy them as one, or bind them with the written system if they must be sequenced.

Empty states in the product are part of the brand. The first time a new customer sees the product, it is empty. That screen should sound like the site. Same sentence structure, same name for the object, a clear next action. An empty state written by a different team in a different decade is how the seam survives an otherwise careful launch.

## One backlog, two surfaces

Keep a single list of decisions that touch both. A rename, a new object, a pricing change, a color change. When the product adds an object the site advertises, the site updates in the same release, or the site waits to advertise it. Shipping the claim first is how you invent a seam on purpose.

Review both surfaces when you review either. A design critique that only opens the marketing frames will approve a tone the product cannot keep. A sprint that only polishes the app will leave the homepage in the old voice. Put both URLs in the same check. Click from the pricing page into the product on a staging account. Read the words on each side of the door.

Ownership helps. One person, or one small team, should be allowed to reject a mismatch. If marketing can ship headlines the product lead has not seen, you will get slogans. If product can rename a button the site still sells, you will get confusion. The shared vocabulary note is the tool. The owner is the person who insists it is used.

Engineering can support the share. Design tokens for color and type, used by the site and the product, stop the slow drift of almost-the-same blues. Tailwind, if both sides use it, makes that practical. Tokens do not fix vocabulary. They fix the easy visual half, so you can spend attention on the words.

A client portal for files does not replace this. The portal can hold the brand note. The product and the site still have to load the same decisions. A PDF of the palette that neither codebase uses is a memory, not a system.

## Sequence without a seam

You can ship the site before the product is public, or the reverse. You cannot ship them as unrelated identities and plan to “align later.” Later is when both have customers who learned the old words. Align the sentence and the type before the second surface is public, even if the second surface is small.

A credible sequence: the sentence and the palette, a site that explains the product honestly, and a product first-run that uses the same words. If the product is too thin to match the site’s promises, cut the promises. A smaller true site is a better front door than a wide one opening onto a different building.

Pricing, docs, and support mail are surfaces too. A help article that uses the old noun will undo the sprint. When you change a name, search the docs and the templates. The maintenance plan for the site should include this search, or the product team will be the only ones who know the current language.

Measure the seam by watching a new user, even informally. Ask them what they think the main object is called, once on the site and once after login. If the words differ, you have your next edit. You do not need a large study to hear a mismatch you wrote yourself.

## The practical test

Open the homepage and the product side by side. Check the action color, the headline face, and three nouns. Click the primary call to action and see whether the next screen could be a continuation. Read the empty state aloud next to the hero. Any sentence that would embarrass one side if the other side heard it is a defect.

Then look at mobile. The seam is often worse there, because the marketing page was designed as a tall story and the product as a cramped port of desktop. The words can still match. If they do, the density difference is forgivable. If they do not, the small screen makes the break obvious faster.

After the two surfaces agree, someone still has to keep them from rotting. [A maintenance plan after launch](/blog/a-maintenance-plan-after-launch) is the next piece. It names who updates the framework, watches the forms, and renews the domain, which is the same kind of ownership the shared vocabulary needs.

If the site and the product are both in front of you and you want to see whether they can be one project, [book an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the two URLs and the list of nouns. The call should leave you with one list, or with a clear reason they are still two brands.
